title: Bobby Deol Made the Best-Reviewed Hindi Film of the Year. Then the Theatres Tried to Bury It.
excerpt: Anurag Kashyap's 'Bandar' went from a Toronto Film Festival standing ovation to a screen-sharing war with the multiplex chains. The film fighting hardest to be seen is the one you should see.
body:
Picture the scene: Toronto, September 2025, the Special Presentations lineup at one of the world's most prestigious film festivals. The lights come up on Bandar, and a fading Bollywood star named Bobby Deol — yes, that Bobby Deol, the one who spent two decades as a punchline before Animal made him terrifying again — is being hailed for the most complex performance of his career. "I never imagined a film of mine will go to a festival," Deol said at the premiere, and you could hear the disbelief in it.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xUWRx5FQzFE

Nine months later, that same film is fighting for its life against PVR, Inox, and Cinepolis. Welcome to the brutal arithmetic of an Indian box office summer.

Bandar — released internationally as Monkey in a Cage — is Anurag Kashyap's gritty crime drama about Samar, an aging television star accused of rape by his ex-girlfriend and swallowed whole by India's judicial machinery. It is, by near-unanimous critical agreement, the best-reviewed Hindi release of 2026 so far. And it walked straight into June, the most crowded month Bollywood has ever assembled — four Fridays, nine major releases, over ₹1,400 crore at stake.

""I never imagined a film of mine will go to a festival," Deol said at the premiere, and you could hear the disbelief in it."

The collision was ugly. According to a report by Bollywood Hungama, Zee Studios made a deliberately modest ask: three to four shows in multiplexes with four or five screens, in slots after 1 PM. A smart, targeted release on 500 to 600 screens, built to grow on word of mouth. Instead, because the national chains were busy distributing the competing films themselves, Bandar was offered scraps. So Zee Studios did something rare — it pulled the film from the major multiplex chains entirely rather than accept what it called an unfair deal.

!Bobby Deol — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

"The logic was to build the film's presence through positive word of mouth, allowing it to have a long run at the box office rather than a crowded opening day." — Girish Johar, Distribution and Revenue Head, Zee Studios

And here's the part that should make every studio executive uncomfortable: the strategy is working. After a modest Friday opening, Bandar jumped nearly 200 percent on Saturday, with evening and night shows reporting packed houses across the country. Not because of spectacle or franchise muscle or a marketing blitz — but because people who saw it told other people to go. In an industry that has surrendered almost entirely to pre-sold IP, sequels, and event films, Bandar is that increasingly rare animal: an original, content-led drama that audiences are choosing to reward.

The craft backs up the conviction. Kashyap, the Gangs of Wasseypur auteur who built his reputation on uncompromising, scrappy, naturalistic filmmaking, is being called more assured here than he's been in years — closer to the director his fans have been waiting for than even his low-key Kennedy delivered. The writing comes from Sudip Sharma and Abhishek Banerjee, the team behind Paatal Lok, Kohrra, and Udta Punjab — pedigree that practically guarantees moral discomfort done well. The supporting cast is a quiet South Indian flex: Sanya Malhotra, Raj B. Shetty, Indrajith Sukumaran, and Natesh Hegde all leave marks, with the prison-set cameos drawing particular praise.

Bobby Deol himself? Critics are split in the most flattering way possible. He delivers what's being described as one of the most restrained, emotionally layered turns of his recent career — a man watching his privilege rot in real time. One of the teaser's standout moments has him in a flamboyant disco-era look, dancing to a reimagined Come On Baby Dil Kisko Degi, before the whole thing curdles into something far darker. It's the kind of swing only an actor with nothing left to prove and everything left to reclaim would take.

The film isn't flawless. Some critics note Kashyap takes too clear a side on the central #MeToo question, draining the story of the ambiguity that might have made it truly explosive, and that the female characters aren't written sharply enough to push back. But even its detractors land on the same verdict: this is an incredibly watchable, purposely dark film that refuses to make things easy.

For the diaspora, Bandar is exactly the kind of title that rewards seeking out. Released worldwide by Zee Studios on June 5, it's the sort of festival-bred Hindi drama that NRI audiences in the US, UK, and Canada tend to embrace once it hits streaming — and given Zee's involvement, a ZEE5 berth feels inevitable in the coming weeks. Watch for it.

In a month built for noise, the quietest, hardest-fought release on the board might be the only one worth remembering.
